sweep_summary: Two target items, both by Faraclas on Rivers Pidgin English (= Nigerian Pidgin nige1257). (1) Faraclas 1984, SLS 14(2):67-76 — already held by the project from the compilation of 9/16 (Illinois OCA djvu text of the volume), read in full: word-level 'stress' of English-derived words is a lexical H on the English-stressed syllable, realized as a stress-like contour only at the end of a pitch phrase / stress-accent group; substrate words are tonal; conclusion = mixed tone / pitch accent / stress system with accentuation at the phrase level. Confirms the catalog's PHRASAL coding. (2) Faraclas 1985, 'Rivers Pidgin (Creole) English..', Studies in African Linguistics Supplement 9 (ACAL 15 précis, ed. Schuh) — downloaded this search of works with stress in the title as the open full-issue PDF from journals.flvc.org (DOI 10.32473/sal.v16iSupp; saved as ): a three-page précis of the SLS paper at pp. 111-113 (Glottolog's '67-76' is the SLS article's pagination, wrong for the supplement); same analysis ('phrase-level system of accentuation which is clearly stress-related'), confirms. Neither supersedes the catalog's deciding source, Faraclas 1996 (Routledge grammar), which is the same author's fuller later statement. Two on-disk extras read for completeness: Faraclas 2013 APiCS survey (confirms phrase stress + lexical tone; states the unmarked-word default H on the penult) and Oyelere 2021 thesis (instrumental; rejects word stress, argues lexical pitch accent + tone, puts Faraclas' stress at the postlexical level — refines, does not contradict). Nothing left to acquire; priority none across the board. all look-ups were done with direct download/automated download against Glottolog and the SAL OJS site.

new_statements.reading: Faraclas' first-hand 1984 analysis of the Rivers (Port Harcourt) dialect: English-derived words keep a lexical high pitch on the syllable that is stressed in English, but this shows up as a stress-like HL contour only when the word ends a pitch phrase (stress-accent group); elsewhere the H spreads rightward, and substrate-derived words are fully tonal and immune to phrase accentuation. The domain of accentuation is the phrase, the within-word peak is lexically specified (tone), and F0 is the only cue. This is exactly the phrase-stress-over-lexical-tone system that the catalog's deciding source (Faraclas 1996, the Routledge grammar) states in full, so the catalog's PHRASAL coding stands. The 1985 SAL Supplement 9 précis (downloaded and read this search of works with stress in the title, pp. 111-113, not 67-76 as Glottolog lists) is a three-page summary of the same paper and adds only the yam/market phrasal-stress minimal pair.

tone_statements.citation: Akinbo, Samuel Kayode. 2025. Iconicity of grammatical tonal polarity and reduplication in Nigerian Pidgin. Journal of Linguistics 61(2): 473-498. doi:10.1017/S0022226724000276
tone_statements.quote: Naijá is tonal like all documented Nigerian languages, except Fulfulde. The language contrasts two tones – namely, H(igh) and L(ow) – and the tonal contrast is illustrated with the minimal pair in Table 1. As shown in the table, H tone is marked with an acute diacritic and L tone with a grave diacritic. The language also has tone contours which are restricted to bimoraic or utterance-final syllables. For example, the word [fᴐ́] ‘four’ surfaces with an HL glide [fᴐ̂] in an utterance-final position.

tone_statements.citation: Yakpo, Kofi. 2021. Creole prosodic systems are areal, not simple. Frontiers in Psychology 12: 690593. doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2021.690593
tone_statements.quote: All African English-lexifier creoles have been described as tonal. Krio (e.g., Berry, 1970; Hancock, 1971; Nylander, 1984; Finney, 2004), Pichi (Yakpo, 2019a), and Nigerian Pidgin (Faraclas, 1996) have been analyzed in detail, showing the presence of equipollent 2-tone systems with fully specified H and L tones, fixed word-tone patterns and tonal minimal pairs. Most English-derived words have a culminative and obligatory H.

tone_statements.quote: Faraclas (1996: 264) postulates two types of distinctive tones in NigP, and each of them has contour allotones. The basic tone-bearing unit in Nigerian Pidgin is the syllable … Underlyingly, syllables may bear a high tone, a low tone or no tone at all. High tone has two allotones: (a) a spreading falling tone or high-low sequence that is borne by stressed syllables, and (b) a level high tone that occurs in all other environments. Low tone has two symmetrically opposite allotones: (a) a spreading rising tone or low-high sequence that is borne by stressed syllables and (b) a level low tone …

sources.citation: Faraclas, Nicholas. 1985. Rivers Pidgin (Creole) English: tone, stress, or pitch accent language? In Russell G. Schuh (ed.), Précis from the 15th Conference on African Linguistics (UCLA, 1984), Studies in African Linguistics Supplement 9, pp. 111-113. (Glottolog ref 59395 gives 'Suppl. 9, 67-76' — the page range is wrong: 67-76 is the SLS 14(2) article; the précis is at pp. 111-113 of the supplement, checked in the issue TOC and body.)
sources.quote: The argument for a stress analysis of pitch phenomena in RPE is supported by the existence of a phrase-level system of accentuation which is clearly stress-related, the limited scope and primarily grammatical nature of almost all critical pitch distinctions in the language, and the clear correlation of stress placement over English words to the assignment of high pitch over most RPE words derived from English. An apostrophe precedes a syllable which receives phrasal stress-accent: /jam/ ['ja:m] 'yam' [a si maket 'ja:m] 'I found the market yams' /maket/ ['maket] 'market' [a si jam 'maket] 'I found the yam market' [p. 111]
sources.locator: pp. 111-112, secs. 1.1 'Arguments for a stress analysis' and 2 'RPE: A mixed system'
sources.note: Three-page conference précis of the SLS paper (same author, same data, same conclusion): accentuation is phrase-level ('phrasal stress-accent' on the final word of an accent group), the placement of the lexical high pitch inside English-derived words mirrors English stress, substrate-derived words are tonal and exempt from phrase-level stress-accent, F0 is the only reliable phonetic cue; the system is declared mixed (tone + pitch accent + stress). Adds nothing beyond the 1984 article except the yam/market phrasal-stress minimal pair. Not a separate description; Faraclas himself cites the work…

tone.quote: Like many West African creoles, Naijá has also been described as having a sparse system of lexical tone with several mostly monosyllabic minimal pairs distinguished by pitch. However, this debate does not appear fully settled … This thesis will not go as far as to argue whether Nigerian Pidgin is or is not a tone language, but it does offer a tool which we hope will nourish such debates going forward. … previous descriptions of Naijá prosody generally support the existence of lexical tone, though some aspects of the language may be coherent with a stress-based analysis.

tone.quote: At the lexical level for example, Naija’s different varieties have been variously described as tonal, as stress, or as pitch accent languages (Mafemi 1971, Obilade 1976, Oyebade 1983, Faraclas 1996, Elugbe & Omamor 1991). … These English source words are used by Naija speakers who also speak any of about five hundred and fifty (550) different local tonal languages, which all have different tonal patterns (Blench 2012). tone.quote: Faraclas (1996: 264) postulates two types of distinctive tones in NigP, and each of them has contour allotones. The basic tone-bearing unit in Nigerian Pidgin is the syllable … Underlyingly, syllables may bear a high tone, a low tone or no tone at all. High tone has two allotones: (a) a spreading falling tone or high-low sequence that is borne by stressed syllables, and (b) a level high tone that occurs in all other environments. Low tone has two symmetrically opposite allotones: (a) a spreading rising tone or low-high sequence that is borne by stressed syllables and (b) a level low tone …
tone.locator: p. 230, section 5.5.3 'Types of distinctive tones in NigP and their allotones'; downstep at p. 237
tone.summary: Adopts Faraclas: two level tones, high and low, on the syllable, falling/rising allotones under phrase stress; English words often bear one tone; downstepped H on emphatic o; F0 study: de H, dè L.
